children.text: The birthplace of Philippine diving, set in the Verde Island Passage, considered the center of the world's marine biodiversity, Anilao is the go-to dive town for divers hunting nudibranchs and rare macro creatures, reachable from Manila by car in just
3 hours

Anilao is the name given jointly to the western coastline of the Calumpan Peninsula in Mabini, Batangas Province, and the waters around Maricaban Island off Tingloy on the opposite side. Since the 1960s and 70s, Manila divers have come here every weekend, making it one of the birthplaces of Philippine leisure diving, and today dozens of dive resorts line the peninsula's coast.

The waters off Anilao lie within the Verde Island Passage, between Luzon and Mindoro. Marine biologists call it "the center of the center of the world's marine biodiversity," a stretch of sea considered to hold the densest concentration of coral and fish species anywhere on the planet, packed into a narrow area. In
, the international ocean conservation group Mission Blue designated the passage a Hope Spot.

Anilao's fame comes less from large fish than from small creatures. Nudibranchs, colorful sea slugs, have been recorded in the hundreds of species here, earning the site the nickname "Nudibranch Capital," and macro creatures that photographers dream of — frogfish, seahorses, ghost pipefish, blue-ringed octopuses, mimic octopuses — are common. At night, blackwater (bonfire) diving, in which photographers shoot transparent larvae rising from the deep, draws underwater photographers from around the world.

Being close to Manila, it's the most popular spot for weekend diving, Open Water certification courses, and underwater photography practice, and there are several Korean-run dive shops as well. That said, it's not a resort with a stretch of white sand beach — most of the coast is rock and pebbles — so it suits travelers looking for underwater exploration rather than beach relaxation.
A mecca for muck diving — hunting small creatures over sand and debris. At sites like Secret Bay and Basura, a single dive can turn up dozens of nudibranch species.
Signature coral sites that are also great for beginners. Twin Rocks is rich with schools of fish and coral, while Cathedral Rock is known for an underwater cross and its coral garden.
A dive done after dark, drifting over deep water with a hanging light to observe plankton and larvae. Recommended for experienced divers, and it must be done with a specialized guide.
A small island shaped like a Mexican sombrero, with coral in the shallows, so companions who don't dive can still enjoy snorkeling.
You can complete pool and open-water sessions within 2–3 days. Some shops offer instruction in Korean, making it a good place to earn your first certification.

On the third day, it's good to do an expedition dive at sites off Tingloy Island or just relax at Masasa Beach. Before flying, leave at least
18–24 hours
after your last dive.

130km

Many dive resorts and shops run pickup vans from Manila. With enough people, it costs about
per person one way, and it's the most convenient option if you're carrying heavy gear.
To cross to Tingloy Island, take a shared bangka from the Anilao pier (about
30–45 minutes
) or use a resort's chartered bangka.
Anilao can be dived year-round, but the sea is calmest from
October to May
March–May
in particular is considered peak season, with calm waters and good visibility. During
December–February

, the northeast monsoon (Amihan) blows, roughening some sites and dropping water temperatures to around 23–25°C, so a 5mm wetsuit is recommended. This period actually sees more nudibranchs, making it popular with macro photographers.
June–September

sees frequent rain from the southwest monsoon (Habagat) and typhoon effects, with rough waves on the Balayan Bay side on many days. When a typhoon warning is issued, the coast guard halts departures and all diving stops. If you travel during this period, keep your dates flexible.
Water temperature runs roughly 23–30°C, and visibility is usually

, varying with currents and plankton conditions. Resorts fill up on weekends, especially long holidays, so a weekday visit is more pleasant. Book accommodation early during the annual underwater photography competition season.

and may vary depending on local conditions.
Most accommodation is dive resorts, typically bundling a room, meals, and diving into a package. Budget places start around
per person per night with meals included, while boutique cliffside resorts with great views run
or more a night. Resorts cluster along the coast at San Teodoro, Bagalangit, and Solo in the south of the peninsula, with dive sites just
5–15 minutes
away by boat. Korean-run resorts offer the advantage of Korean food and Korean-language instruction.

There aren't many restaurants outside the resorts, so most meals are taken there. Local Batangas dishes include bulalo (rich beef bone-marrow soup), lomi (beef noodle soup), and the strongly aromatic kapeng barako coffee. Stop by a lomi specialty restaurant on your way back through Batangas City or Lipa.
Book the dive shop in advance, and be sure to bring your logbook and certification card (or digital proof). If it's been a while since your last dive, ask for a refresher dive.
If your goal is macro photography, it's worth hiring a dedicated muck-diving guide. An eye for spotting creatures makes all the difference to your results.
ATMs are very scarce around Anilao. Bring cash for dive fees, environmental fees, and tips. It's safer to withdraw money in Batangas City beforehand.
Mobile signal weakens the further south you go on the peninsula. Resort wifi is often slow, so check in advance if you need to stay connected for work.
SLEX traffic is heavy on Sunday afternoons heading back to Manila. Either do only a morning dive and leave before lunch, or set off early Monday morning.
For companions who only want to snorkel, arranging a separate outing to Sombrero Island or Masasa Beach keeps them from getting bored.
Get diver insurance (such as DAN) in case of an accident. It's also a good idea to check the location of the nearest decompression chamber with the shop.
Bring supplementary lighting for underwater photography, spare batteries, and moisture absorbers. Coastal humidity causes gear failures often.
Don't trek up Mt. Gulugod Baboy or cross a high pass right after diving. Even a small gain in altitude raises the risk of decompression sickness.
Many sites in Anilao waters can suddenly develop strong currents. Don't dive solo without a guide, and always carry a surface marker buoy (SMB).
Touching coral or wildlife, or moving them for photos, is prohibited. Fines can be imposed in marine protected areas.
Venomous creatures such as blue-ringed octopuses, lionfish, and stonefish are common. Don't touch the bottom with your hands, and maintain neutral buoyancy.
When a typhoon warning or a coast guard departure ban is issued, all boat diving stops. Build slack into your schedule.
There are periods when jellyfish are common, so a full wetsuit or rash guard is recommended over a short-sleeve suit.
